reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes OneCoin as an investment, directs viewers to a registration destination, and describes paying for token packages while projecting substantially higher proceeds from later coin sales. The described outcome depends on package-specific selling limits and future availability, including a higher daily selling allowance for a larger package, alongside token, bonus, credit, invited-participant, and automated-purchase mechanisms.

Nevertheless, if I sell all 500 coins for five euros, I will get 2500 euros.

opening.argument: The speaker presents this as a personal decision rather than a guaranteed recommendation. He repeatedly qualifies the outlook: the price may rise only "once every 10-20 years," the future is uncertain because "Time will tell!", and he leaves the choice to the viewer, saying, "Everyone choose the life for himself." He also explains why he personally is not withdrawing money, rather than promising that every viewer will profit. That combination of conditional language, personal framing, and explicit uncertainty is more consistent with investment commentary containing risk than with a deceptive guarantee.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The registration line and optimistic title show promotion, but they do not establish a guarantee or concealment. The speaker expressly uses uncertainty, including "maybe" and "Time will tell!", and says viewers must decide for themselves. The cited selling limit also shows a qualification to the projection, not proof that the speaker represented withdrawal as unrestricted or certain.

citations.quote: OneCoin - the best investment in 2015!
perhaps at the end of March it will cost 6 euros
because it is a selling limit, of course.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Conditional wording does not neutralize the central message: viewers are shown paid token packages and projected resale proceeds. The speaker says he paid for tokens, received coins, and could obtain substantially more by selling them. Calling the increase possible or saying "Time will tell!" softens certainty but still presents appreciation as the reason to participate, while the registration link supplies a route to do so.

opening.argument: The video's primary function can be understood as a demonstration of the speaker's own accounts and reasoning. The title frames it as an explanation of a personal non-withdrawal decision, and the speaker says he is answering friends who asked that specific question. He walks through account amounts, token counts, sale limits, and possible timing, inviting the audience to inspect how the calculations work. That is an experiential account or operational demonstration of a platform's displayed balances and rules, not necessarily a directive that viewers must buy.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The fact that the speaker answers friends does not make the material instructional or neutral. The description explicitly calls OneCoin "the best investment," and the narration moves beyond account description into expected prices and proceeds. A demonstration can still be promotional, but the cited material does not show an explicit audience instruction to purchase or a claim that the outcome is guaranteed.

citations.quote: OneCoin - the best investment in 2015!
perhaps at the end of March it will cost 6 euros

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The account walkthrough is not merely technical: it links paid packages to token acquisition and then calculates what selling those tokens could yield. The speaker also says he will wait for a higher price and describes adding money to multiple accounts. A personal demonstration can function as solicitation when its instructional detail illustrates an attractive investment outcome and is paired with a registration destination.

opening.argument: The evidence describes a product-like account and token system, but it does not establish the additional mechanism needed to call the presentation a scam. It does not show a guaranteed return, a required deposit from the audience, credential collection, or downline income. The speaker discusses his own purchases and limits, says he sells only when profitable for him personally, and frames the decision as individual. The visible account dashboard and transaction history are consistent with demonstrating an ordinary service interface, while the supplied material does not establish that the registration URL was used or what it led to.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The reference points to purchases and projected resale, but those facts alone can describe a commercial token service without proving deception. Its quotes do not show that viewers were required to deposit funds, that returns were guaranteed, or that the speaker earned from recruiting them. The URL is labeled a registration destination, yet the supplied record does not establish that anyone followed it or what service appeared there.

The evidence directly connects payment to token packages, receipt of coins, a stated token price, and hypothetical resale for a much larger amount. The description also calls OneCoin an investment and provides registration access. Whether the link was used or whether recruitment income appears does not change that the core claim is token purchase followed by appreciation-based proceeds.
